title: Longing for union (IV.13)
hook: the soul longs to be one with Christ in the sacrament
tomorrow: thirty days in one little book. which line will you keep?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the front step of book four: the invitation is real, and so is the awe. The line was come with reverence.

A holiday dinner on a video call. You can see the table, hear the forks and the laughing, and you can't pass the salt. What do you do when you can't get to the table? Catholics who can't receive communion, because they're sick, or far away, or not able to receive, have an old answer. They make a spiritual communion: they tell Christ they long for him, and ask him to come into the heart.
screen: `A DINNER ON A VIDEO CALL.` → `YOU CAN'T PASS THE SALT.` → `A SPIRITUAL COMMUNION.`

segments.voice: The question underneath is old: is wanting God already a way of being near him? Chapter thirteen of book four answers with pure longing. Who will grant me, the disciple asks, to find you alone, to open my whole heart to you, and talk as a friend talks with a friend? He borrows Isaiah, in the Douay-Rheims: "Verily thou art a hidden God." Near in the sacrament, and hidden, so the longing grows instead of fading. He asks to be set on fire and made one spirit with Christ. That's union in this book: closeness so deep the words run out. Now a neighbor who knows this ache. The psalms belong first to the Hebrew Bible, and Psalm 42 in the Jewish numbering says it like this, in the Douay-Rheims, where it's Psalm 41: "As the hart panteth after the fountains of water; so my soul panteth after thee, O God." In the Jewish Publication Society's translation, the next line asks when the psalmist will come and appear before God. Jews and Catholics both pray this psalm, a thirst for the living God. And one honest difference: in book four, the longing is for Christ, present in the sacrament, a belief Jewish tradition doesn't hold. Same thirst, read in two houses. Here's the thing to say at dinner tonight: some of the same words of longing are prayed in a synagogue and a church.
screen: `IS WANTING GOD A WAY OF BEING NEAR?` · `VERILY THOU ART A HIDDEN GOD.` · `AS THE HART PANTETH.` · `SAME THIRST, TWO HOUSES.` · then, large: `ONE WITH HIM.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and let one wanting be there without pushing it into a feeling: a person you miss, a place you can't get to, or God. Breathe slowly and stay near the wanting itself. Catholics who pray may make a spiritual communion here, in their own words.
Longing for union. Book four's wish to be one with Christ in the sacrament: near, hidden, and wanted with the whole heart.
Hold on to this: one with him, and the longing itself is part of the closeness. Go gently.

howItsDone: Catholics who cannot receive communion, at home, in hospital or watching Mass from afar, can make a spiritual communion, telling Christ of their desire to receive him; Jews and Christians both pray the psalms, including Psalm 42.

chat.meaning: The psalms belong first to the Hebrew Bible; Jews and Catholics both pray them. Shared thirst, with an honest difference about the sacrament.

Unity thread (wisdom day): Psalm 42 (Jewish numbering) shared by Jewish and Catholic prayer; the JPS 1917 line 'When shall I come and appear before God?' is paraphrased, not quoted. Honest difference: the Imitation's longing is for Christ present in the Eucharist, which Jewish tradition does not hold. No ranking. Jewish Keeper should confirm the framing.
Spiritual communion: Council of Trent, Session XIII ch. 8, speaks of those who receive spiritually by desire. 'An old answer' kept vague on purpose; confirm.
